The house faces the incoming wind. Move it into the lee of a ridge.

Contours respond to the three ridges, overall slope, and low ground. Closed contours rise inward; closer lines indicate steeper ground. A narrowing between high areas is a saddle, while contours bending toward higher ground can indicate a valley. The airflow remains a two-dimensional teaching approximation—not CFD, geotechnical analysis, or a hydrology report.

II · Four observations

The environment answers directly.

風

Blocking is not sealing.

A barrier deflects air and may create a gentler leeward zone. Too close or too dense, it can also leave stagnant pockets.

雨

Water goes downhill.

Risk rises when a house sits on a drainage line. Elevation and a clear outflow path matter more than the mere presence of water.

日

Orientation negotiates with the sun.

Move through a day. Orientation decides when light enters; trees and eaves trade summer shade against winter sun.

人

Covered behind, open ahead.

Prospect–refuge theory describes a preference for shelter behind and view ahead. Here both become visible quantities.

III · Name the pattern

The old term is feng shui.

“气乘风则散，界水则止。古人聚之使不散，行之使有止，故谓之风水。”Common text of the Book of Burial: qi disperses when carried by wind and stops at the boundary of water.

This page places observable wind, light, heat, water, and spatial experience on one field.

IV · A typical form

Backed and embraced, with room ahead.

The diagram returns common form-school terms to observable environmental relations. It is a modern reading framework, not a claim that historical concepts equal engineering categories.

Feng shui termPosition in the layoutEnvironmental reading
Backing mountain
靠山		Main ridge behind the houseMay block part of the incoming wind and provide a sense of cover. A gentle ridge extension often drains better than a collecting hollow; actual foundation stability still requires geotechnical investigation.

面水		River in frontHistorically associated with water supply, transport, view, and open space, but always accompanied by flood, erosion, and dampness risks.
Azure Dragon east
White Tiger west		For a south-facing house, east is left and west is rightSide barriers may reduce crosswinds and create a milder field; poor spacing can also accelerate canyon winds or create stagnant air.
Bright hall
明堂		Open ground between house and riverOpen communal space, a daylight face, an activity ground, and a clear prospect.
Holding wind, gathering qi
藏风聚气		Area enclosed by backing and side ridgesReduce extreme wind and form a tolerable microclimate. The aim is not zero air movement but avoidance of both violent and stagnant air.
Dragon vein
龙脉		Continuous ridges and valleysA way to observe mountain chains, divides, watersheds, and landform continuity—not a claim about a hidden physical energy channel.

V · Reduced to essentials

What remains when the terms are stripped away?

For a place meant to support life over time, four judgments remain: adapt, keep flows healthy, balance competing needs, and fit people to environment.

IADAPTATION

Work with nature

Read climate, terrain, water, sun, and wind; place roads, houses, trees, and water systems with them rather than against them.

IIFLOW

Maintain movement

Air, water, people, and resources must move—neither stagnating nor rushing without control. Cang feng ju qi describes gentle flow with useful pause.

IIIBALANCE

Seek proportion

Sun and shade, ventilation and shelter, openness and enclosure have no single maximum—only a fit for a particular place.

IVHUMAN–ENVIRONMENT FIT

Let place and people fit

Environment shapes health, feeling, behavior, and social life; people continually reshape it in return.

In plain termsgood daylight · moving air · no violent wind · stable ground · less dust · human comfort
